placard_text: A detailed model of a Chinese ocean-going junk with watertight bulkheads and battened sails. Vessels like this carried silk, porcelain and tea across the South China Sea to Southeast Asian ports.
A brass astrolabe used by sailors to measure the height of the sun and stars above the horizon. It helped captains find latitude on long voyages around Africa to the spice islands.
A merchant ship's logbook recording winds, ports, crew illness and cargo of pepper and cloves. Its cramped handwriting shows how dangerous and profitable the spice trade was.
An ink and colour scroll showing junks and foreign merchants crowded at the harbor of Hoi An. Japanese, Chinese and European traders met here to exchange silk, ceramics and silver.

A wooden model of a dhow with a triangular lateen sail, built without nails and stitched with coconut fibre. Dhows rode the monsoon winds between Arabia, India and East Africa carrying incense and cloth.
theme_tags: maritime, ship, monsoon, trade, indian ocean

placard_text: A hand-written manifest listing Chinese silk, porcelain and Mexican silver loaded onto a galleon crossing the Pacific. The route linked Asia and the Americas for more than two hundred years.
A floating needle compass in a lacquered bowl marked with directions. Chinese sailors used magnetic compasses at sea long before they appeared in European ports.
Bowls, jars and bronze ingots recovered from a sunken trading vessel off the Vietnamese coast. The cargo preserves a snapshot of everyday commerce between kingdoms.
A parchment sea chart covered with crossing compass lines and the names of ports written along the coast. Portolan charts guided Mediterranean captains before modern mapmaking.
A hand-painted map of the southern Chinese coast showing harbors, islands and sailing routes. Officials used it to watch trade and defend against pirates.
A page from an early Vietnamese atlas showing provinces, rivers and mountain passes in ink. It reveals how the court surveyed its territory and organised roads.
A hand-coloured star map showing constellations drawn as animals and heroes. Navigators and astronomers used charts like this to track the night sky.
A decorated map tracing overland routes from China through Central Asia to the Mediterranean. Small illustrations mark caravanserais where merchants rested camels and traded goods.
theme_tags: maps, trade, silk road, caravan, geography

placard_text: A tall porcelain vase painted in cobalt blue under a clear glaze with swirling lotus flowers. Kilns in Jingdezhen produced such vases for the court and for export across Asia.
A bowl with a soft green celadon glaze and a delicately carved lotus pattern inside. Potters fired it in a wood kiln to create the cool jade-like colour admired by scholars.
A large Vietnamese jar painted in underglaze blue and decorated with a stylised dragon. Chu Dau kilns exported ceramics to Japan, the Philippines and the Middle East.

exhibit_title: Export Porcelain Plate with European Crest
placard_text: A Chinese porcelain plate ordered by a European family and painted with its coat of arms. It shows how potters adapted designs to suit overseas customers.
A spouted ceramic kendi used to pour water without touching the lips. These vessels travelled on trading ships and were popular from Java to the Philippines.
theme_tags: ceramics, trade, vessel, southeast asia, pottery

placard_text: A glazed pottery camel carrying bundles of goods, coloured in amber, green and cream. Figures like this were placed in tombs to honour travellers on the Silk Road.
theme_tags: ceramics, silk road, tomb, china, glaze

placard_text: A panel of painted tiles with tulips and carnations in red and turquoise on a white ground. Ottoman workshops in Iznik used them to decorate mosques and palaces.
A tin-glazed earthenware vase with multiple spouts for displaying tulips. Dutch potters copied Chinese blue-and-white porcelain that arrived on merchant ships.
A silk robe woven with gold thread and clouds, waves and dragons. Only high officials could wear such patterns, and the weavers' skill reflects centuries of the silk industry.
A cotton cloth painted with a flowering tree and fixed with mordant dyes that stay bright after washing. Indian chintz was traded across Asia and Europe in exchange for spices and silver.
A silk panel embroidered with phoenixes and peonies in tiny satin stitches. It once decorated a screen in a palace room and took a team of embroiderers many months.
A carpet with a central medallion and thousands of knots per square inch. Persian workshops made carpets for shahs and for merchants who exported them along the caravan routes.
theme_tags: textiles, carpet, persia, weaving, silk road

placard_text: A cotton cloth patterned by drawing hot wax on the surface and dipping it in indigo and brown dyes. Each motif carries a meaning, and some designs were reserved for royalty.
A suit of lacquered iron plates laced with silk cords, topped by a crested helmet. It protected a warrior while allowing movement on horseback and in battle.
A bronze blade decorated with fine patterns and fitted to a long shaft for use in warfare. It comes from the Dong Son culture, famous for casting skilled metalwork.
A double-edged steel sword with a cross-shaped guard and a leather-wrapped grip. Knights trained for years to use it in battle and in tournaments.
A bronze cannon cast to defend a merchant ship against pirates and rival fleets. Armed trading vessels fought for control of harbors and sea lanes.
A steel helmet with engraved gold decoration and a spike on top, worn by an officer in the sultan's army. The inscriptions praise courage in battle.
A bronze Buddha sitting in meditation with a calm expression and a lotus base. Pilgrims left offerings in front of statues like this in temples.
A sandstone relief of a dancing goddess from a Cham temple tower. The carving shows how Hindu beliefs shaped sacred architecture along the central coast.
A gilded silver box shaped like a small cathedral, made to hold a saint's relic. Pilgrims travelled long distances to see such sacred objects.
A copper cylinder filled with paper scrolls of mantras that turns on a wooden handle. Each spin is believed to send prayers into the world.
A limestone slab showing a family offering to the gods, with hieroglyphic text above. Households kept small shrines like this to honour deities and ancestors.
A bronze food vessel with animal masks and thunder patterns, used in ancestor ceremonies. Skilled casters made them in clay molds for kings and nobles.
A massive bronze drum with a sun at the center, rings of birds and scenes of boats and warriors. It was struck during ceremonies and also served as a symbol of authority.
